lead: Hebrews sets two pictures side by side: priests who stand day after day offering sacrifices again and again, and Christ who, after one offering, has sat down at God's right hand. Luke tells of a great dinner where everything is ready and the invited guests make excuses, so the host fills his house with the poor and with strangers from the roads. The sacrifice is complete, the table is set, and the invitation is still going out. This evening the Third Sunday after Qyomtho begins. The key words are single offering, ready and come.

set: This passage closes the long central section of Hebrews on Christ's priesthood and sacrifice (chapters 7–10). In 10:1–10 the writer has said that the law's sacrifices, repeated year after year, could not take away sin, and that Christ came to do the Father's will, offering his own body “once for all” (10:10).
Now the writer returns to the promise of Jeremiah 31 he quoted in chapter 8, and lets the Holy Spirit's own words close the argument.
str: v. 11: every priest stands, offering again and again.
vv. 12–14: Christ, after a single sacrifice, sat down.
vv. 15–17: the witness of the Spirit in Jeremiah's promise.
v. 18: where there is forgiveness, there is no longer an offering for sin.
kw: The offering of Christ on the Cross is one and is never repeated. Its effect reaches all times.
The Greek perfect tense describes an action complete in the past whose result lasts. What Christ did once remains effective.
The participle is present: “those who are being made holy”. The one sacrifice is finished; our sanctification goes on as we receive it.
vv: And every priest stands day after day at his service,
In the sanctuary of the old worship there was no seat for the priest. His work was never finished.
But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, “he sat down at the right hand of God,”
Sitting means the work is done, and it means royal authority (Psalm 110:1). The risen Christ reigns and intercedes.
For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are sanctified.
The whole of salvation is contained in this one sentence: one offering, all time, all who are being made holy.
Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin.
No new sacrifice can be added to Christ's. Every Christian offering is a sharing in his.
ch: The Catholic Church teaches that the Eucharist does not repeat or add to the sacrifice of the Cross, but makes that one sacrifice present. “The sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice”, with the same victim and the same offerer, now offering through the ministry of priests (CCC 1367, following the Council of Trent). So when the Holy Qurbono is offered, the one sacrifice of Hebrews 10 is made present among us, and its fruits are given to us.

r.h: Come, for everything is ready now
set: The setting is still the sabbath meal at the house of a leader of the Pharisees (14:1). One guest, hearing Jesus speak of the resurrection of the righteous, exclaims how blessed are those who will eat bread in the kingdom. Jesus answers with a parable that asks whether we will come when we are called.
In that world, a host sent a first invitation and then, when the meal was ready, a servant to call the guests. To refuse at the last moment was a public insult.
str: vv. 16–17: the dinner and the call: “Come.”
vv. 21–23: the poor and the strangers brought in.
kw: The main evening meal, here a feast. It is an image of the banquet of the kingdom that the prophets foretold (Isaiah 25:6).
To ask to be let off. All three excuses are polite, and all three put something good, land, oxen and marriage, before the host.
A strong word, but in the customs of the East it describes pressing an invitation on someone who is too humble to accept. The disciples at Emmaus “urged him strongly” in the same spirit (Luke 24:29).
vv: Blessed is anyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!
A pious wish about the future. Jesus turns it into a question about the present: you are invited now.
Come; for everything is ready now.
Everything has been prepared by the host. Nothing is asked of the guests except to come.
Go out at once into the streets and lanes of the town and bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame.
The same four groups Jesus told his host to invite (14:13). God does what he asks us to do.
and compel people to come in, so that my house may be filled.
The host wants a full house. The urgency is the urgency of love.
ch: The parable is a warning to every hearer, and first of all to the baptized, not to let good things keep us from God's table. It must never be read as God rejecting a whole people. Some in past centuries used “compel them to come in” to justify forcing people into the Church. The Church today teaches clearly that no one may be forced to embrace the faith against his will, because the act of faith is by its very nature voluntary (Dignitatis Humanae 10; CCC 160). The only compulsion the Gospel knows is the pressure of a warm invitation.

qa: If Christ's sacrifice is complete, why do we offer the Holy Qurbono every day?

Not to add to the Cross, but to receive it. The one sacrifice of Christ is made present in the Holy Qurbono, so that each generation can share in it and receive its fruit (CCC 1366–1367). Hebrews says there is no other offering for sin; the Holy Qurbono is not another one but the same, offered in the way the Lord commanded at the Supper.
study: Christ “sat down” because his work was finished. Where am I still trying to earn what he has already given?
Which of the three excuses sounds most like mine? What is keeping me from the Lord's table?
